problem_plain: Building and running AI systems at scale requires solving a wide set of infrastructure problems that do not fit neatly under any single hardware category: training models across many machines without choking on network bottlenecks, keeping the software that runs those models from ballooning in size, shrinking the memory needed to store optimizer state during training, making measurements of system performance honest and comparable, accounting for the carbon cost of building and running chips, and compressing the enormous datasets that feed these systems. Each of these is a distinct engineering challenge, yet all of them quietly limit how fast or how cheaply AI can actually progress. Together they form the unglamorous plumbing that determines whether the theoretically possible hardware improvements translate into real-world gains.
why_plain: AI workloads are physically constrained by two scarce resources that money cannot infinitely buy: memory capacity and communication bandwidth. Every workaround that wastes either one — bloated software libraries, redundant optimizer state, slow data synchronization across continents, or uncompressed data streams — costs real time and energy at scale.
approach_plain: Researchers across these papers attack infrastructure inefficiency from multiple angles simultaneously: pruning away software that is never actually used, mathematically approximating expensive optimizer bookkeeping with cheaper surrogates, redesigning how gradient synchronization happens across slow wide-area network links, compressing raw data at wire speed so less bandwidth is needed in the first place, and replacing misleading aggregate performance statistics with ones that are mathematically correct. The common thread is finding and eliminating hidden waste — in software, in memory, in network round-trips, in how results are reported.

groups.heading: Shrinking memory used during model training
groups.explain: Training a large language model requires storing not just the model weights but also the optimizer's running statistics — numbers that track how each weight has been changing, used to set each weight's personal learning rate. For a 7-billion-parameter model these statistics alone occupy 28 gigabytes, crowding out space for data and forcing the use of more machines. The papers here find clever ways to store far less without changing what the training process actually learns.

papers.name: APOLLO
papers.gloss: Replaces the full per-weight optimizer statistics with a compressed low-rank approximation, cutting optimizer memory from 28 GB to 1.6 GB for a 7B-parameter model while matching training quality; enables 3x higher throughput by fitting larger batches on the same hardware.

groups.heading: Training across slow or unreliable network links
groups.explain: Standard distributed training requires every machine to share its gradient updates with every other machine after every single training step, which works fine inside a data center on fast private cables but becomes a bottleneck when machines are in different cities or connected only by ordinary internet. The papers here redesign the synchronization pattern so that machines do many local steps before talking to each other, dramatically cutting how much data must cross the slow link.

papers.name: Photon
papers.gloss: Lets geographically distributed clusters each train locally for many steps before synchronizing, reducing network traffic 500-fold for a 7B model and cutting total training wall-clock time 35% versus a centralized approach, while actually improving model quality.

papers.name: JaxPP
papers.gloss: Extends the JAX machine-learning framework to support flexible pipeline parallelism schedules (where model layers are split across machines and data flows through them like an assembly line), enabling efficient multi-machine training across slower inter-node links.

groups.heading: Removing dead weight from machine-learning software
groups.explain: The software libraries that power GPU-based machine learning ship with enormous amounts of compiled code — kernels for dozens of GPU architectures, operations for every possible workload — but any given training run uses only a tiny fraction of it. This dead code consumes memory, slows down program loading, and wastes the scarce capacity of the GPU's own memory. The paper here builds a tool to identify what is actually used and strips out the rest.

papers.name: Negativa-ML
papers.gloss: Intercepts the runtime calls that load GPU compute kernels to discover which ones any given workload actually uses, then permanently removes the rest from the library files; shrinks GPU code by up to 75% and cuts peak GPU memory use by up to 70%.

groups.heading: Compressing scientific and AI data at wire speed
groups.explain: Scientific simulations and large AI datasets produce floating-point numbers — the kind of decimal values computers use for real-world measurements — in volumes that outpace storage and network bandwidth. Compressing these numbers before storing or sending them buys back that bandwidth, but existing compressors force a choice between speed and compression ratio. The paper here closes that gap specifically for floating-point data on both CPUs and GPUs.

papers.gloss: Four new lossless compression algorithms tuned to the internal bit structure of floating-point numbers, achieving over 500 GB/s throughput on a modern GPU while beating most existing compressors on compression ratio too.

groups.heading: Accounting for the carbon cost of building and running hardware
groups.explain: The environmental cost of a chip comes from two places: the energy consumed while it runs (operational carbon) and the enormous industrial process that manufactured it (embodied carbon — the carbon baked into the chip before it ever turned on). These two costs trade off against each other in ways that are easy to ignore. Chips with more transistors are faster but cost more to fabricate; running fewer, larger chips longer saves manufacturing carbon but may use more electricity. The paper here builds a framework to optimize both costs together.

papers.name: CORDOBA
papers.gloss: Defines a single combined metric — total carbon times execution time — that captures both manufacturing and operational carbon, then uses it to prune 98% of chip design options; finds that stacking memory directly on top of the processor die improves this combined metric 6.9x.

groups.heading: Making performance measurements honest and comparable
groups.explain: Researchers report speedups by averaging ratios across many benchmarks, but the standard averaging method (the geometric mean) is mathematically wrong for speedup ratios: it can declare one design faster than another even when the opposite is true in any single workload. Meanwhile, specialized hardware for tasks like VR eye-tracking is evaluated with its own domain-specific metrics. The papers here address measurement correctness at the methodology level.

papers.gloss: Proves algebraically that the geometric mean misrepresents aggregate speedup and that the harmonic mean is the correct replacement; shows that the two can give opposite rankings for competing chip designs.

papers.name: POLO / POLONet
papers.gloss: Co-designs an eye-tracking neural network with a dedicated hardware accelerator that renders VR images at full quality only where the user is actually looking, cutting end-to-end latency 3.9x versus prior gaze-tracking approaches.

Speeds up GPU-based text pattern matching (used in database queries and log analysis) 19.5x by reordering computation so each block of input text is loaded once instead of once per pattern, eliminating redundant memory traffic.

connect: Every paper here ultimately fights the same root constraint: the gap between how fast processors can compute and how fast data can move to feed them. Whether the fix is compressing data before it travels, eliminating optimizer state that occupies precious memory, synchronizing gradients less often across slow networks, or stripping unused code that crowds out working data — each solution reclaims bandwidth or capacity that arithmetic alone cannot create.
